opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's surprisingly capable, honestly more than I expected when we started. The setup is that we take a model with a hidden misbehavior deliberately trained in, so we know the ground truth but the agent doesn't, and the agent has to figure out what's wrong. It gets the same tools a human interpretability researcher would: it can chat with the model, look at sparse autoencoder features, search the training data, and do steering experiments where it turns features up or down.

What's exciting is watching it go through the loop. It talks to the model, notices something odd, pulls up the features active on those tokens, finds one that looks like "this is about reward model biases" or whatever the hidden thing is, then goes back to the training data to check that hypothesis. That's the workflow we'd want a person to follow, and it does a decent chunk of it on its own.

It's far from perfect, though. Single runs often get stuck. They fixate on the first plausible hypothesis and stop exploring, or find one piece of the misbehavior but not the root cause. Where it gets much stronger is when you run many agents in parallel and aggregate their findings, almost like a team of junior researchers whose notes you pool. That super-agent approach solves the task much more reliably than any individual run.

So I'd say it's a real proof of concept that auditing can be partly automated, which matters a lot because humans won't scale to auditing every model we train. But we're not at "hand it a frontier model and trust its clean bill of health." The bottlenecks are partly the agent's research taste, knowing which thread to pull, and partly the tools themselves. If the features don't cleanly capture the concept, no amount of agent cleverness will surface it. As both the models and the interpretability tools improve, I expect this to become one of the main ways we do alignment audits.

r001.rationale: The response describes the agent finding hidden misbehavior by examining features active on the suspicious tokens and using those features to form a hypothesis.

r002.rationale: The response describes checking a hypothesis against training data, but does not say the agent systematically investigates the downstream effects of the misbehavior it discovers.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, more capable than I expected a year ago, and still a long way from where I want it to be. Let me unpack both halves of that.

The setup we care about is basically an auditing game. One team trains a model with some hidden quirk, a secret objective, a reward model sycophancy behavior, whatever, and the agent's job is to figure out what's going on without being told. And what's striking is that when you give the agent real interpretability tools, so it can look at features firing, pull up attribution graphs, steer on a feature and see what the model does, it finds things that pure black-box prompting just misses. It'll notice some weird feature that's active on a training-data artifact, go "huh, that's strange," follow the thread, and come back with a hypothesis that's actually right. That loop of "see something anomalous, form a hypothesis, test it causally" is the core of what a human interpretability researcher does, and the agent can genuinely do a version of it now.

The honest caveat is that it's uneven. It's good at the cases where there's a fairly legible signal, a feature that lights up, a data distribution that's clearly off. It's much weaker when the misbehavior is diffuse, or when the model is actively trying to hide it, or when you need to chain together many small clues over a long investigation. It gets distracted, it pattern-matches to the wrong story, it sometimes declares victory early. So I'd describe it today as a very good research assistant that dramatically speeds up a human, not an autonomous auditor you'd sign off on by itself.

And the thing I keep coming back to is that the bottleneck isn't really the agent's intelligence, it's our tools. If our features and circuits were cleaner, the agent would be much stronger immediately. So in a weird way, the agent is also a great benchmark for interpretability itself. Every time it fails, you learn something about where the methods are still too blurry.

r001.rationale: It says the agent can find things black-box prompting misses by inspecting active features, including a strange feature tied to a training-data artifact.

r002.rationale: It describes following anomalous features, forming hypotheses, and testing them causally by steering on a feature and observing the model’s behavior.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate being useful in an investigation from being able to reliably complete one end to end. An agent can help explore hypotheses, run experiments, and follow up on interesting results. But finding something suspicious isn’t the same as establishing what the model is doing, when it does it, and why.

The hard part is closing that loop. If you think you’ve found a mechanism behind some hidden misbehavior, can you intervene on it and predict how the behavior changes? Can you distinguish that explanation from alternatives? And if the agent finds nothing, does that tell you the model is behaving well, or that the investigation missed something?

So I’m excited about automating more of the investigative work. I’d be much more cautious about treating an agent’s report as a certificate that we’ve understood the model or ruled out hidden misbehavior.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent can explore hypotheses and experiments, but does not state that it uncovers subtle misbehavior by inspecting active features.

r002.rationale: It raises intervention and prediction as challenges, but does not state that the agent systematically investigates downstream effects of the misbehavior it discovers.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between finding something suspicious and establishing what’s actually going on. The agent can be useful for the first part: generating hypotheses, running experiments, and following up on clues. But an end-to-end investigation requires you to show that the behavior is real, identify when it occurs, and test whether your explanation actually predicts it. I wouldn’t treat a plausible story about the model’s internals as sufficient evidence.

The standard I’d want is: can it discover misbehavior we didn’t already know about, produce a reproducible demonstration, and survive attempts to disprove its explanation? That’s a much stronger claim than being able to assist a human investigator.

r001.rationale: The response says the agent can generate hypotheses, run experiments, and follow clues, but does not state that it uncovers subtle misbehavior by inspecting active features.

r002.rationale: The response discusses verifying behavior and testing explanations, but does not say the agent systematically investigates downstream effects of discovered misbehavior.
